items.title: Kenya : des empreintes vieilles de 1,43 million d’années livrent de nouveaux indices sur les premiers humains
items.description: Une equipe de chercheurs a decouvert une serie d'empreintes fossilisees sur le site archeologique de GaJi10, dans la region orientale du Turkana, au Kenya. Datees d'environ 1,43 million d'annees, elles comptent parmi les ensembles de traces les plus complets jamais mis au jour pour etudier le comportement d'anciens representants de la lignee humaine. Selon Arkeonews, dans un article publie le 28 juillet et consacre a une etude parue dans la revue scientifique Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences , les chercheurs ont recense 21 empreintes reparties en cinq pistes continues. Elles auraient ete laissees par huit individus. Le site a egalement livre 146 traces d'animaux, notamment d'hippopotames, de bovides, d'oiseaux et d'equides. Leur presence montre que de nombreuses especes frequentaient les abords de cet ancien lac. La plupart des hominides avancaient dans la meme direction a travers une zone peu profonde, tandis qu'un autre marchait en sens inverse. Rapidement recouvertes de sable fin puis de sediments, les empreintes sont restees suffisamment bien conservees pour permettre une analyse detaillee. Contrairement aux ossements, qui peuvent s'accumuler sur de longues periodes, ces traces ont enregistre un moment precis. Elles offrent ainsi une image directe des deplacements de plusieurs individus presents au meme endroit. Une identification encore incertaine L'analyse en trois dimensions a revele une voûte plantaire plus plate et un gros orteil davantage ecarte que chez l'etre humain moderne. Selon Arkeonews, ces caracteristiques se rapprochent de celles attribuees a Paranthropus boisei , une espece ayant vecu en Afrique de l'Est entre 2,3 et 1,2 million d'annees environ avant notre ere. L'estimation de la taille des individus figure parmi les elements les plus surprenants de l'etude. Certains auraient pu atteindre environ 1,80 metre, soit davantage que ce qui etait generalement admis pour Paranthropus boisei . Ces dimensions restent neanmoins compatibles avec Homo erectus , egalement present dans la region a la meme epoque. Les auteurs de l'etude precisent donc qu'il n'est pas encore possible d'attribuer les empreintes a une seule espece, meme si leur morphologie semble davantage correspondre a Paranthropus boisei . Plusieurs individus auraient marche ensemble L'orientation des pistes apporte egalement des indications sur le comportement de leurs auteurs. Selon Arkeonews, plusieurs individus, probablement de grands mâles, auraient pu avancer ensemble. Cette hypothese pourrait renseigner sur leur organisation sociale. Les chercheurs restent cependant prudents, car ces traces ne suffisent pas a reconstituer avec certitude le fonctionnement de leurs groupes. Pour les auteurs de l'etude, l'interet de la decouverte tient surtout a la nature meme des empreintes. Les fossiles osseux renseignent sur l'anatomie, tandis que ces traces montrent directement comment plusieurs hominides se deplacaient dans leur environnement.

items.title: Le Royaume du Maroc et la République du Mali réaffirment leur volonté d’imprimer un nouvel élan au partenariat stratégique entre les deux pays
items.description: Le Royaume du Maroc et la République du Mali réaffirment leur volonté d'imprimer un nouvel élan au partenariat stratégique entre les deux pays Bobo-Dioulasso, 28 juil. 2026 (AIB) -À l'occasion de la tenue, du 21 au 24 juillet 2026 à Bamako, de la 4e session de la Grande Commission mixte de coopération maroco-malienne, les deux parties ont réaffirmé, vendredi dernier, leur volonté commune d'insuffler une nouvelle dynamique au partenariat stratégique entre le Mali et le Maroc, afin de hisser davantage leurs relations économiques, commerciales et de coopération, a appris l'AIB auprès du ministère des Affaires étrangères, de la Coopération africaine et des Marocains résidant à l'étranger. Selon le compte rendu du ministère des Affaires étrangères, de la Coopération africaine et des Marocains résidant à l'étranger, la 4e session de la Grande Commission mixte de coopération maroco-malienne a été coprésidée par le ministre des Affaires étrangères, de la Coopération africaine et des Marocains résidant à l'étranger, Nasser Bourita, et le ministre des Affaires étrangères et de la Coopération internationale de la République du Mali, Abdoulaye Diop. Lors de cette session, qui a permis aux deux parties de procéder à un examen approfondi de l'état de leur coopération bilatérale dans les différents secteurs, les deux ministres se sont félicités des liens profonds de fraternité et d'amitié qui unissent les deux pays et ont réitéré leur volonté commune de faire des relations maroco-maliennes un modèle de coopération interafricaine, fondée sur les valeurs de solidarité, de respect et de partage, conformément à la vision et à la volonté communes de Sa Majesté le Roi Mohammed VI et du président de la Transition, chef de l'État de la République du Mali, le général d'armée Assimi Goïta. Dans le domaine économique et commercial, les deux parties ont souligné l'importance du renforcement des échanges entre les opérateurs économiques maliens et marocains et se sont félicitées de la tenue du Forum des affaires organisé en marge de cette session, qui a permis d'identifier de nouveaux domaines d'intérêt commun et de convenir d'actions concrètes visant à renforcer les relations d'affaires entre les deux pays. Les deux parties se sont également félicitées du renforcement du cadre juridique régissant leur coopération bilatérale, à travers la signature de plusieurs accords de coopération, et ont réitéré leur engagement à assurer le suivi de leur mise en œuvre, en vue de consolider davantage les relations privilégiées entre le Royaume du Maroc et la République du Mali. Dans le communiqué conjoint adopté à l'issue de la 4e session de la Grande Commission mixte de coopération maroco-malienne, la République du Mali a réitéré sa « position en faveur de l'intégrité territoriale et de la souveraineté du Maroc sur l'ensemble de son territoire, y compris la région du Sahara », tout en réaffirmant son appui au Plan d'autonomie présenté par le Maroc, comme étant « la seule solution crédible et réaliste pour la résolution de ce différend régional ». En marge des travaux, le ministre Nasser Bourita a été reçu en audience par le général d'armée Assimi Goïta, président de la Transition, chef de l'État de la République du Mali. Lors de cette audience, le chef de l'État malien a remercié Sa Majesté le Roi Mohammed VI pour la position constante et cohérente du Royaume du Maroc en faveur de la souveraineté, de l'unité nationale et de l'intégrité territoriale de la République du Mali. Agence d'Information du Burkina

items.title: Les travailleurs compressés réclament plus de 18 milliards de FCFA à l’État malien
items.description: Des milliers d'anciens travailleurs maliens attendent toujours le paiement integral de leurs droits. Reunis au sein de l'Association des compresses du Mali, ils attendent toujours le versement de plus de 18 milliards de francs CFA par l'etat. Les travailleurs compresses du Mali denoncent la lenteur dans l'execution de cette decision obtenue en 2016. Le president de leur association, Ousmane Berthe, rappelle que le dossier a traverse plusieurs regimes politiques. « ca fait dix ans et c'est l'execution d'une decision de justice qu'on a recue en 2016, un arret. Alors avec le regime IBK, on a fait les quatre ans. Avec la transition, six ans encore de negociations. » Un accord trouve mais sans suite Le representant de ces ex-employes affirme qu'un consensus a pourtant ete trouve avec les autorites sur le montant a verser. Selon Ousmane Berthe, un protocole commun a ete elabore, mais le ministere de l'economie et des finances n'a pas encore donne suite. « On est convenu sur les 18 milliards, on est convenu d'un protocole commun et jusqu'a present, le ministere des finances n'a pas reagi. » Tout en reconnaissant les difficultes auxquelles le pays est confronte, le president de l'association estime que cette situation ne doit pas empecher le reglement du dossier. « D'accord, le pays est en crise, c'est vrai, mais nous sommes des travailleurs aussi qui a peine on arrive a survivre, on vit peniblement. On avait deja paye, mais c'est le reste maintenant », confie monsieur Berthe avant d'indiquer que « la totalite des compresses va a 52 000 travailleurs, mais ceux qui sont concernes par ca (ce dossier Ndlr) vont a 32 000 travailleurs. » L’article Les travailleurs compressés réclament plus de 18 milliards de FCFA à l'État malien est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .

items.title: «23,7% de femmes et de filles sont victimes de violence»
items.description: Les acteurs de lutte contre les violences basées sur le genre sont en conclave pour deux jours dans la capitale du Pakao. L’objectif : renforcer le mécanisme de coopération pour l’assistance des victimes. SEDHIOU- En Casamance, les acteurs de la lutte contre les violences faites aux femmes et aux filles multiplient les stratégies pour éradiquer ce mal. Sous l’égide du ministère de la famille de l’action sociale et des solidarités, les forces de sécurité, les agents de santé et de la justice, acteurs de la communication et de la protection sociale ont démarré ce mercredi un atelier de deux jours dont l’objectif est de mettre en place un système de prise en charge intégré. Un instrument qui va renforcer « le protocole de pris en charge des multisectoriel regroupant cinq ministères élaborés et valider par la tutelle pour alléger la démarche des victimes », a indiqué Rokhaya Diop, chargé du programme d'éradication des violences basées sur le genre, au ministère de la famille de l’action sociale et des solidarités. Selon, elle une étude menée par l’agence nationale de la démographie a révélé 31,9% des femmes sont victimes de violence au Sénégal, 23,7% à Sédhiou, a-t-elle poursuivi. Un taux de prévalence est élevé qui explique la tenue d’un atelier dans le cadre du projet de l'élimination des violences faites aux femmes et aux filles. Rappelant l’enjeu de ce phénomène, Ba Ousmane Dalnfakha, adjoint au gouverneur de la région de Sédhiou a souligné la responsabilité d’apporter une assistance aux victimes : « lorsqu’une femme ou une fille est victime d’une violence, elle doit bénéficier d’une prise en charge appropriée, l’accueil et l’orientation jusqu’à la prise en charge sanitaire psychosocial et judiciaire ». Il a insisté à cette occasion sur la nécessité de renforcer la sensibilisation des communautés afin de réduire durablement les violences faites aux femmes et aux filles. La rencontre a réuni les acteurs de Sédhiou, Kolda et de Ziguinchor pour deux jours. Jonas Souloubany BASSENE (correspondant)

items.title: Sandbondtenga/Chefferie traditionnelle : le Naaba Koom II prend officiellement possession de son palais à Napalgué
items.description: Sandbondtenga/Chefferie traditionnelle : le Naaba Koom II prend officiellement possession de son palais à Napalgué Kaya, 27 juillet 2026 (AIB)-Le Naaba Koom II, nouveau chef du canton de Diguila, a officiellement intégré, samedi dernier, son palais royal à Napalgué, chef-lieu dudit canton, au cours d'une cérémonie solennelle dénommée Nakinsgo (entrée au palais), marquant l'aboutissement du processus traditionnel de son accession au trône. La cérémonie du Nakinsgo a été ponctuée de salutations coutumières, d'hommages des notables ainsi que des délégations venues des villages du canton et des cantons frères et alliés. Les visiteurs, porteurs de présents destinés au nouveau locataire du palais, ont célébré l'événement dans une ambiance festive. Intronisé le 27 juin 2026 à Boussouma, le Naaba Koom II intègre ainsi officiellement son palais après avoir accompli les rites traditionnels du retour royal, un périple de vingt-huit jours à travers plusieurs localités conformément aux usages ancestraux. Après avoir présenté ses allégeances et sa gratitude à Sa Majesté le Naaba Sigri, Dima de Boussouma, au lendemain de son intronisation, le nouveau chef s'est rendu auprès du chef de Bigsi, son logeur traditionnel, avant d'entreprendre son itinéraire rituel. Son parcours l'a conduit successivement à Goulguin, Kougrin-Sian, Rasla, Tampelga, Gounghin, puis à Napalgué, où il a été reçu par le Banaaba et le Dapor-Naaba avant de rejoindre définitivement son palais, d'où il exercera désormais son autorité coutumière. À chacune des étapes, l'autorité coutumière a reçu les honneurs qui lui sont dus, en présence des notables, des autorités coutumières et des populations fortement mobilisées. Âgé de 45 ans, Ouédraogo Pingrwaooga Youssouf à l'état civil, professeur des écoles en service dans la région d'Oubri, succède, selon la volonté du Roi Sigri, à son père, feu le Naaba Simbdo, décédé le 21 décembre 2025 après quarante-deux années de règne à la tête du canton. En accédant au trône sous le nom de Naaba Koom, porté autrefois par le huitième chef du canton et signifiant « eau », symbole de vie et de fertilité, le dix-huitième chef de Diguila hérite d'une responsabilité à la fois historique, sociale et morale. Après plus de quatre décennies de règne de son prédécesseur, les populations du canton placent en lui l'espoir d'une gouvernance coutumière fidèle aux valeurs ancestrales tout en étant attentive aux défis contemporains. Le canton de Diguila est l'un des douze cantons du Royaume de Boussouma, l'un des grands royaumes mossis du Burkina Faso, placé sous l'autorité suprême du Dima, Sa Majesté le Naaba Sigri. Il tire ses origines du Naaba Kuilga, fils du Moogho Naaba Kouda. Il partage ainsi une ascendance commune avec plusieurs cantons voisins, notamment Soubeira, Piktenga et Kirgoutenga, liés par la parenté et la tradition. Agence d'Information du Burkina AIO/ata

items.title: Sandbondtenga/Éducation : la solidarité entre le primaire et le secondaire à Pensa saluée lors de la Journée de l’excellence scolaire
items.description: Sandbondtenga/Éducation : la solidarité entre le primaire et le secondaire à Pensa saluée lors de la Journée de l'excellence scolaire Kaya, 12 juillet 2026 (AIB)-La Direction provinciale de l'Enseignement secondaire et de la Formation professionnelle et technique (DPESFPT) du Sandbondtenga a décerné, le 12 juillet 2026 à Kaya, une attestation de reconnaissance au chef de la Circonscription d'éducation de base (CEB) de Pensa, Samuel Sawadogo, pour son engagement en faveur de la relance de l'enseignement secondaire dans cette commune confrontée à de forts défis sécuritaires. Selon Hamadé Tinto, directeur provincial de l'Enseignement secondaire, de la Formation professionnelle et technique, cette reconnaissance consacre une collaboration exemplaire entre les deux ordres d'enseignement, qui a permis d'assurer la continuité de l'éducation à Pensa malgré un contexte difficile. « Entre le secondaire et le primaire dans le Sandbondtenga, il n'y a pas de limite », a-t-il déclaré. Il a expliqué que les échanges engagés avec le chef de la CEB avaient permis de définir une stratégie commune pour relancer le Collège d'enseignement général (CEG) de Pensa. « Le CCEB est venu dans mon bureau et nous avons discuté de comment faire pour que l'éducation reprenne au secondaire dans cette commune. Grâce à ce travail conjoint, l'école a fonctionné correctement, primaire comme secondaire, jusqu'à la fin de l'année », a-t-il souligné. Pour le directeur provincial, « c'est cette solidarité et cette collaboration parfaite qui ont donné les résultats tangibles dont nous nous réjouissons aujourd'hui », justifiant ainsi la remise officielle de cette attestation de reconnaissance. Recevant sa distinction des mains de Barkebila Sawadogo, directeur provincial de l'Enseignement préscolaire, primaire et de l'Éducation non formelle, Samuel Sawadogo a rappelé que l'enseignement secondaire avait pratiquement cessé d'exister à Pensa depuis la crise sécuritaire de 2019. « Nous avons accompagné l'enseignement secondaire dans la commune, qui n'existait même plus depuis la crise en 2019, à rouvrir cette année scolaire », a-t-il indiqué. Il a évoqué les nombreuses difficultés rencontrées, notamment le manque de matériel didactique, de fournitures scolaires et de salles de classe. « Personnellement, je me suis dit que l'éducation ne doit pas s'arrêter face à ces difficultés », a-t-il affirmé. L'inspecteur a précisé avoir soutenu le collège à travers la cantine scolaire afin de favoriser le maintien des élèves et de renforcer le moral de l'équipe éducative. « C'est ça la résilience », a-t-il soutenu, rappelant que les personnes déplacées internes installées dans la commune « ont, elles aussi, réellement besoin de l'éducation ». Remerciant les autorités éducatives pour cette marque de confiance, Samuel Sawadogo a estimé que cette distinction constitue une invitation à renforcer davantage la collaboration entre les acteurs de l'éducation, en particulier dans les zones à fort défi sécuritaire, afin de garantir la continuité des apprentissages du primaire au secondaire. Agence d'Information du Burkina IO/aio/ata

items.description: Sandbondtenga/Paix : le MPAP annonce la 6e édition des Ambassadeurs de Paix Awards à Boussouma Boussouma, 26 juillet 2026 (AIB)-Le Mouvement pour la Culture de la Paix et l'Amour de la Patrie (MPAP) a annoncé, samedi à Boussouma, la tenue de la 6ᵉ édition des Ambassadeurs de Paix Awards (APA 2026), prévue les 30 et 31 juillet, sous le thème : « Face aux défis sécuritaires, l'amour de la patrie comme force d'unité et de cohésion sociale ». Selon le MPAP, Boussouma a été choisie pour accueillir cette conférence en raison de son attachement aux valeurs traditionnelles et de son symbole de rassemblement. Face à la presse, Paul Marie Zoma, président du MPAP, a indiqué que cette édition vise à promouvoir le patriotisme, la cohésion sociale et le dialogue comme réponses aux défis sécuritaires que traverse le Burkina Faso. « Cette édition se veut une réponse citoyenne aux défis sécuritaires », a-t-il déclaré. Pour Amado Soudré, président du comité d'organisation, l'édition sera marquée par des panels, des échanges et des distinctions à l'honneur des acteurs engagés pour la paix et le vivre-ensemble. Les organisateurs ont appelé les médias à accompagner cette initiative en relayant « les messages de paix, de cohésion sociale, de solidarité, de patriotisme et d'espérance » pour contribuer à « un Burkina Faso plus résilient et plus fraternel ». En marge de cette conférence, les organisateurs ont rendu une visite de courtoisie à Sa Majesté le Naaba Sigri, Dima de Boussouma, patron de l'édition. Agence d'Information du Burkina OW/aio/ata

items.title: Protection sociale : le gouvernement reçoit le RSUG
items.description: Le gouvernement gabonais a officiellement réceptionné le Registre social unique du Gabon (RSUG), un outil structurant destiné à améliorer l’identification et la prise en charge des populations vulnérables. Déployé dans le cadre du programme Gabon Digital, ce dispositif marque une étape clé dans la modernisation et l’efficacité des politiques de protection sociale. Photo de famille à l’issue de la cérémonie ce 29 juillet 2026. © GabonReview Ce mercredi 29 juillet, en présence du représentant du vice-président du gouvernement (VPG), de certains membres du gouvernement, de la Banque mondiale, la ministre des Affaires sociales, Armande Longo épse Moulingui a reçu le Registre social unique du Gabon (RSUG) qu'elle a ensuite remis au représentant du VPG et à ses collègues du gouvernement. Cette cérémonie inscrite dans le cadre du programme Gabon Digital, levier stratégique de transformation de l’action publique, a été marquée par la présentation de la matrice combinée des programmes et des cibles, du parcours du bénéficiaire de la Protection sociale non contributive (PSNC), ainsi que du dispositif législatif associé. Mieux prendre en charge les populations vulnérables Au cœur de cette initiative, une ambition claire : améliorer les mécanismes de prise en charge des populations vulnérables, avec une attention particulière portée aux femmes. Conçu comme une base de données dynamique et interconnectée, le RSUG permettra d’identifier avec précision les personnes en situation de vulnérabilité et d’adapter les interventions publiques en matière de santé, d’alimentation et d’accompagnement social. « Ce registre sera un mécanisme efficace du sommet à la base », a affirmé la ministre des Affaires sociales, insistant sur son impact attendu dans le renforcement du cadre institutionnel. Armande Longo remettant le document au chef de cabinet et représentant du VPG. © GabonReview Les livrables stratégiques remis aux autorités traduisent cette nouvelle approche intégrée. Ils comprennent notamment un parcours bénéficiaire structurant l’ensemble du processus de prise en charge, depuis l’accueil et l’identification jusqu’à l’évaluation des résultats et l’autonomisation ; une matrice combinée permettant de planifier les interventions en définissant les populations prioritaires, les objectifs et les indicateurs autour de programmes d’assistance et d’un volet dédié à l’autonomisation ; ainsi qu’un projet de réforme législative visant à adapter le Code de protection sociale afin d’institutionnaliser le Registre social unique du Gabon. Plateforme consultable en ligne Jusqu’ici, l’absence d’outils fiables d’évaluation limitait l’efficacité des politiques sociales. Désormais, grâce à une plateforme consultable en ligne par les travailleurs sociaux et les administrations, il sera possible de mieux cibler les bénéficiaires et de coordonner les actions. La vulnérabilité est définie conformément à la loi 1/2018, en lien avec le seuil de pauvreté multidimensionnelle en cours d’ajustement. Le déploiement du RSUG se fera de manière progressive, avec notamment la mise en place prochaine d’un formulaire d’enrôlement unique et la possibilité d’inscription en ligne pour les bénéficiaires. Pour Hugues Mbadinga, coordonnateur national du projet, il s’agit d’un outil opérationnel permettant d’orienter concrètement les décisions publiques, notamment dans des situations telles que la scolarisation des enfants issus de familles précaires. Porté conjointement par les ministères de la Planification, de l’Économie numérique et des Affaires sociales, ce dispositif s’inscrit dans la composante 3.2 du programme Gabon digital, dédiée à l’amélioration des services de protection sociale. Il mobilise également d’autres départements clés, tels que la Santé et le Commerce. Avec le RSUG, le Gabon amorce ainsi une transition vers une protection sociale plus ciblée, coordonnée et efficace, fondée sur des données fiables et une approche résolument tournée vers l’action. L’article Protection sociale : le gouvernement reçoit le RSUG est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .

items.title: The Political Fight That Could Decide 2028
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this week’s episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with his reaction to President Trump’s latest round of tariffs and explains why he believes they are weakening America’s economy and its alliances. Then, David is joined by his Atlantic colleague Jonathan Chait for a wide-ranging discussion on the White House Correspondents’ Dinner, whether presidents should be funny, the growing attacks on Barack Obama’s legacy, and the battle in Michigan between moderates and the progressive left that could shape the Democratic Party’s future. Finally, David closes the show with a discussion of Eric Cline’s 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed and the Bronze Age collapse. The following is a transcript of the episode: David Frum: You are kind of an immoderate centrist. You’re ready to—you have centrist views, but you’re ready to brawl. But do you see, as you look at the Democratic Party, that there’s something about the moderate—they will not fight back? And therefore, they’re abdicating by default to people who are going to end up empowering Trump. And whoever Trump’s successor is, probably J. D. Vance, and all that J. D. Vance means for the future of American democracy. Chait: Absolutely. Look, it’s, it’s an old problem, right? The definition of a liberal is someone who’s too broad-minded to take his own side in an argument. This has been something that liberals have noticed about ourselves and have been complaining about ourselves, without doing anything to change, for generations. [Music] David Frum: Welcome to The David Frum Show. I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic. My guest this week will be my Atlantic colleague Jonathan Chait, and we’ll be talking about Obama’s legacy and what it means for the future of American politics. The book this week will be 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed by Eric Cline, a study of the end of the Bronze Age. But before either my dialogue with Jonathan Chait or the book discussion, some opening thoughts on the most recent rounds of tariff announcements by President Trump. Last Friday, President Trump announced his latest tariffs to go into effect. He targeted 60 economies. I say “60 economies,” because one of the 60 targeted was Taiwan, which is not regarded by the United States as a country but only as an economy. So, 60 economies including Taiwan; 59 countries plus Taiwan. The ostensible basis of this new round of tariff increases was to combat forced labor. President Trump used a provision in American law that allows the president power to impose tariffs on countries that use forced or slave labor, and he said: That’s it. In order to fight forced or slave labor, these 60 economies, including Taiwan, are going to be targeted by a new round of tariff increases. The grounds given for the tariffs are not really very plausible. There is no or barely any factual showing that all of these 60 were engaged in some way in forced labor. The United States, after all, is not completely clean on this question either, and there’s no graduation of the tariff to the alleged cause. There’s no saying: Such-and-such country has more forced labor or more openness to forced labor, such-and-such has less; therefore they have different tariff rates. No. It’s just—we accuse these 60 economies, we target them with tariffs, and we’re doing this even though our own hands are not clean. The United States economy is open in many ways to forced labor. Pretty obviously, what is going on here is that Trump is looking for some legal basis to reinstate the tariffs that he has had struck down in the past. President Trump originally used an emergency economic authority from the 1970s. The Supreme Court told him he couldn’t do it. Then he fell back on a temporary provision that allowed him to impose tariffs for a period of time, I think 150 days, and that time has run out. So now he’s looking for what he can get. As the president returns again and again and again to imposing tariffs on the world, a question has to be asked: What on earth could any Trump supporter imagine the president is possibly doing that is, in any way, in the American national interest? The emotional basis, the argumentative basis, the intellectual basis for tariffs is that we are supposedly reindustrializing the United States. But since Donald Trump has become president, manufacturing jobs in the United States have declined by the tens of thousands, probably somewhere between 80,000 and 100,000 net manufacturing jobs fewer as I record in the summer of 2026 than when Donald Trump became president at the beginning of 2025. Because other sectors other employment sectors are continuing to grow, especially health care, this loss of a net 100,000 manufacturing jobs means that manufacturing as a share of nonfarm payrolls has now dipped below 8 percent, which is the lowest level that manufacturing has had in American employment since figures began. Maybe it was lower in 1776 than it is now, but since good figures began, this is the lowest. It’s a record. So obviously, it’s not working. And it’s not just jobs that are being lost. Manufacturing output and manufacturing investment also seem to be in decline. This is a little harder to calculate because there’s a huge capital-investment boom going on because of artificial-intelligence data centers. A lot of money is being committed to these data centers, and the question is: To what extent does this get counted as manufacturing investment and whatnot? But private economists who have tried to separate out seem to be in some kind of agreement that, at best, manufacturing investment is flat in the Trump year and a half, maybe down a little bit, because of the problem of the Trump tariffs. The thing I wish I could pound into the head of tariff supporters is that every tariffed item is not only a product that you sell to consumers; it’s also an input into something else. When you impose tariffs on goods, you make not just things more expensive for American consumers—you make things more expensive for the American companies that buy those things and put them into other things. It’s a house-that-Jack-built problem. Every time you make an input more expensive, you make the ultimate product more expensive and make the final American product that much less competitive on world markets. And the result is: You can’t compete, so you sell less, so you invest less, so you employ less. A large part of the attraction of tariffs to Donald Trump seems to be that they appeal to his desire for dominance. His perception of the world is divided into subjects and into enemies, and if you’re not a subject, then you’re an enemy. And if you’re an enemy, then there are no rules. And if you’re a subject, for that matter, there aren’t any rules either. That everything is an expression of will and ego, and all economics is a matter of I win, you lose, and if I don’t feel I’m winning, then I must be losing. This has become the signature political and economic philosophy of an entire political party under Donald Trump. The party that used to stand for markets and enterprise, the Republican Party, the party of Reagan and Romney. We’re on a bad track here, and these latest tariffs mark another bad milestone on that bad track. We need to get off this, and we need to start creating in freedom and with rules. That doesn’t mean that we pretend that China is not a problem. China is a problem, and there’s forced labor in China. And China is a rule-breaker and steals intellectual property. You need a China-specific solution to the problem of trade, not a solution that destroys the whole apparatus of trade with all of America’s friends and, increasingly, former friends. The United States is now bound in a grinding and frustrating war with Iran. It needs all the friends it can get. The idea that it is waging economic aggression on all of its partners and then acting baffled and befuddled that these partners don’t help out on the Iran problem—a war that the United States started and that it did not have to start and that now it can’t get out of—that just, again, seems to be another bad milestone on another bad path. The way out of all of America’s problems—it’s not the whole solution, but it’s the beginning of a solution—is to return to the path of free and fair trade with friendly-minded nations, bracketing China as a special problem, and otherwise dropping tariffs to the lowest rates possible and returning to the days when the United States negotiated agreements with its friends to trade in freedom and prosperity with mutual benefit and understanding that true trade makes all those who participate in it better off. And now my dialogue with Jonathan Chait. [Music] Frum: Jonathan Chait has dedicated 30 years as one of this country’s sharpest, wittiest, and most ornery advocates for liberalism, first at The New Republic, then at New York magazine , and since 2024 at The Atlantic. It’s a remarkable career made more impressive by the fact that journalism was always his second choice of avocation, adopted only after the involuntary abandonment of his true ambition: head coach of the University of Michigan football team. Jonathan Chait is the author of Audacity: How Barack Obama Defied His Critics and Created a Legacy That Will Prevail. And Jonathan is a continuing reminder that liberalism doesn’t have to be apologetic or bashful about itself. Jonathan, welcome to The David Frum Show. Jonathan Chait: Thank you, David. Frum: Okay, so we have a number of things to talk about today. I want to start—I know this is a topic that’s maybe a little more interesting to me than to you—but to start by looking back at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner that was recorded on Saturday night, just a few days before you and I record. This has always been a kind of troublesome event from a point of view of Washington journalism. There are big advantages to being close to politicians, and big hazards as well. So I know you worked at the glory days of The New Republic when there was a lot of intimacy between The New Republic and the politicians it liked. How do you think about events like the White House Correspondents’ Dinner? And do you think about them differently in the age of Trump from the way you thought about them before? Chait: I was always very skeptical of these events. I went to one to see what it was like, but I felt like if you go to more than one, then you’re no longer going anthropologically; you’re actually part of the thing. And I didn’t want to be part of the thing, because I think it’s a little bit gross. Part of it, just mechanically, is journalistic outlets using themselves as intermediaries for their advertisers to give them access to politicians and to celebrities. The celebrities come because they get some cachet for being at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner. The politicians get access to donors and to celebrities and to journalists. And I feel like it’s cozy for everyone, but I don’t think it’s really good for the journalism profession at all, and never has been. In the Trump era, people have started to question it more than they have, but I feel like The New York Times was correct 20-some years ago to pull out of the event, and I wish everyone else would too. Frum: Trump has changed the ritual in one very noticeable way—which was, in the past, the president’s speech always followed a strict form. Which was a series of gentle jibes at the press, somewhat tougher jibes at himself, occasional jibes at political opponents. That was handled with extreme care. Obama did them more than others, but that was always a little dangerous to do because it sort of violated the treaty of the evening. Followed, of course, by the moment at the end where the politician switches from humor to seriousness and pays tribute to the important role of the press, and everyone likes hearing him say it, whatever the politician may think in the recesses of the politician’s heart. Trump just goes on pure aggression, pure attack. And that may make it easier for journalists to disavow or disconnect themselves from something that was troublesome before. Chait: I think that’s right. What was the most revealing joke he made was actually a decent joke, at least on paper. His delivery was horrible, because he can’t deliver written text. But he made a joke about how he’s basically taken control of CBS News, how he effectuated regime change there and installed Bari Weiss. And that’s actually pretty chilling, right? I mean, that’s the [Viktor] Orbán playbook that we were all warning about in action, and he’s just boasting about it to the faces of the journalists. Frum: It’s also, by the way, self-defeating in a way that Trump’s speeches are often not very strategic. But if it were true that Bari Weiss was the person you had installed at CBS, that is the last joke in the world that a president should make, because it only detracts from the effectiveness of your supposed ally. Which I, again, I don’t think she is. But if she were, it detracts from your effectiveness. It undercuts her. It puts her in an untenable situation. Why would you say such a thing? Trump doesn’t seem always to think those things through Chait: Well, he doesn’t think them through. But I think at some level he’s acting from some instinct to dominate and to make everyone acknowledge the domination, right? He doesn’t work with any subtlety. He actually has to tell people what he’s done and force them to wear the hat on their head. We may not want to go down this path of debating what’s happened at CBS, but I think it’s pretty clear that Trump believes he has done this at CBS. Now, whether Bari Weiss thinks that’s what she’s doing is a different question. Frum: I think you make a very shrewd point. Which is that Trump, even when he would do better to allow dignity to people whom he thinks of as allies—he can’t do it. He has to humiliate; he has to dominate. He has to actually take his friend’s head and dump it in the bucket of shit, and pull the friend’s head out again and say, See, my friend is now covered in shit thanks to me. That’s the kind of guy I am, and this is the kind of low-grade character my friend is. Chait: That’s right. That’s right. I mean, bending the knee is a metaphor people often use, but there’s a visual strikingness to it, right? I mean, an actual sign of submission is what he requires of people who submit to him. David Frum: Now, let me pivot here to the Barack Obama first White House correspondent dinners, and then his presidency. When I wrote speeches for President [George] W. Bush, I occasionally tried to introduce jokes into them. I have this especially vivid memory of writing a joke that—I’m now going to forget what the joke is, unfortunately. But I remember thinking it was quite good, and putting it into a speech, and having the joke be struck by [senior adviser] Karl Rove personally. And when I went to Karl Rove to complain and say the joke was funny, Rove said—and I thought this was very wise—he said, The joke was funny. That’s why I killed it. It was too funny. Presidents shouldn’t be that funny. And one of the things that was very striking when Obama spoke at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner was he was that funny. He said the thing you couldn’t believe a president had said. They were often hilarious, but often sometimes too funny. Did you have qualms about that? Chait: No, I don’t. I think there’s a belief that some people have that humor and insight and dignity are in tension with each other, and I’ve just never thought that. I’ve always thought of humor as an aspect of intelligence. When someone can say something funny, to me that’s a sign that they have some insight that they’re able to express into the world. And I’ve never objected to any figure of any persuasion being funny. [Senator] Ted Cruz, with whom I disagree on almost everything, can often be very, very funny, and I appreciate that about him. I think we need more of it. Frum: Well, let me quote the Obama joke that made me most uncomfortable, but that was very funny. So I believe this was the White House Correspondents’ Dinner just after he had been reelected in 2012, and he was taking a bit of a victory lap, and he mentioned that one particular donor, I think it was Sheldon Adelson, had spent the then-astonishing sum of $100 million to defeat him. And Obama, sort of exulting that it hadn’t worked, said: If he felt that strongly about it, why didn’t he just offer the $100 million to me and ask me to leave politics altogether? I’m not saying I would’ve done it, but I would’ve thought about it. And that was really funny, but it’s— Chait: It’s a great joke. Frum: It’s a great joke, but why is it a great joke? So, there’s a theory that humor is how we adjust discomfort. It’s how we deal with the taboo and discuss the taboo in a way that’s socially acceptable. And so the taboo there is, yeah, politicians could bribe rich people. We’ve reached a degree of wealth in American society where a rich man could say: You know, I don’t like your views. Here’s $10 million. Go to an island. I want you never to be heard from again. And there are politicians who might say, Satchel full of money, airplane ticket in hand, off I go. And when you joke about it, you remind people of that reality. Which we all know, but it’s a little uncomfortable to face. Chait: Or that we’re still banning bribery—at the time, we were still banning bribery. We no longer are banning bribery anymore. But you can spend $100 million. So there’s this last barrier against a rich man’s influence that we can’t cross. So he can go all this way, but he can’t just take the most direct possible route to his ambition. Frum: So you wrote this book about Obama at the very end of the Obama presidency. Trump came to office. You attracted a lot of attack for the book, because how could you say Obama was effective when he was immediately followed by Trump? You spent a lot of the 2010s defending Obama from critics on the right who said he was a communist and a Kenyan, or a Kenyan communist, or a communist Kenyan. Now the attacks seem to come from the left. I know you’re not a person of tender sensibility, but how do you deal with this? Chait: You know, it is interesting, and I have reflected on this, because I would say 75 to 80 percent of the argument I make in the book is against those critics on the right, and maybe 20 percent is against the criticisms of the left. And there were criticisms from the left of Obama at the time, but they were just much, much less important. And what’s interesting in retrospect, as you sort of indicated, is that the conservative critiques have mostly been forgotten, dropped altogether. They’ve just moved on to other things to anger them at the moment. Whereas the left-wing criticisms have survived. They’ve just been repeated over and over again and have established themselves as kind of official histories of that era and are widely believed, even if they weren’t widely believed at the time. And it’s really been fascinating, and I don’t quite have a full handle on how that happened other than just the sheer power of repetition at the time. In other words, to listen to people talk about Obama now, you would think that Obama was just leaving on the table all these left-wing victories he could have been taking because he was just such a neoliberal shill. That he, out of cussedness, just hated Medicare for All and loved Wall Street. But at the time, he was seen as a socialist. And it wasn’t just by the Republican Party. The mainstream media was portraying him as a radical. Let me just give you one example—and there are many examples of this—but the kind of official history we have now of the stimulus is that Obama held down the size of the stimulus because he didn’t want to spend more money on stimulus, because he was worried about the deficit. The truth is that Obama, rightly or wrongly, was trying a strategy to get the maximum stimulus sum he thought he could get out of Congress. And Obama was being seen at the time as being completely irresponsible in pursuing stimulus. The New York Times was treating the deficit as the big crisis and the economic crisis as a secondary problem. It was treating his attempt to stimulate the economy in the face of these deficits as perverse. It was basically running stories saying: We are looking at $100 trillion dollar deficits down the road, and nonetheless, Barack Obama wants to spend even more money. Which is such a hard sell. That was the mainstream narrative that he was fighting against, and the whole context in which he was operating has been completely forgotten. Frum: Well, we were there. And it is true that Obama’s first job as president was saving the banking system and the larger American free-enterprise economy. And maybe he didn’t love that job, but that was the job that history gave him, and that’s what he did. I have a very unusual view on this, which is I actually think that the period from October 2008 to March of 2009—the Bush-Obama transition—is actually one of the finest hours in the history of U.S. government and the finest hours in the history of the presidency. And a remarkable testimony to two men of different backgrounds working together on a common enterprise in ways that were very generous. And the one I think about the most was one of the questions that George W. Bush faced in the fall of 2008 was: Should he save General Motors or not? And there were two obvious choices. One was save General Motors, and do it, and then your predecessor would have to live with it. And the other was, kill General Motors, and then your predecessor would have to live with it. And Bush instead made the decision, save them for 90 days, or prob—well, I would forget the exact number of days, but save them for enough of a period that your successor would have full autonomy to decide for himself whether to save General Motors or not. And indeed, we didn’t have a Great Depression, and we didn’t have the collapse of democratic systems all over the world, and we didn’t have a collapse of world communism, er, world capitalism. We didn’t have global communism. I think of those as good things. Chait: And do you remember the phrase that conservatives applied to the bailout of GM? Gangster. Gangster government was the most common one. Gangster government. This was them indicating that he had gone beyond—they’d already called him a socialist. Now he had gone so far beyond socialism they needed an even viler epithet to describe what he was doing. That these dangerous methods he would use to leverage control of the private sector and basically put us on the road toward communism and improper uses of government power. Frum: I remember very vividly a conversation I had sometime in the spring of 2009 with a group of young, I think they were Koch fellows or some kind of group funded by conservative projects. And I was much more in the conservative world in those days than I am now, although well on my way out because of this. I remember talking to this group of four or five young people, and they were explaining that if it had been up to them, they would’ve allowed the banks to liquidate themselves. So I said, Let’s play that out. And I walked them through—I won’t take time here to do it—but, what happens if you allow a bank liquidation? And that means all kinds of people who had good assets suddenly find they don’t have liquidity sufficient to cover their assets. So even though the assets are perfectly fine, they have to be liquidated hastily to raise capital. And you have this accelerating crisis through the whole economy, which is the story of 1931, ’33. But I played it out for them in very vivid terms. And I remember one of them, as I described this nightmare scenario, getting quite ashen and saying: Well, I guess it’s a good thing we weren’t in power then, because our ideas wouldn’t have worked in an emergency. Chait: Right. Frum: Well, if your ideas don’t work in an emergency—all the ideas work in nonemergency. ( Laughs .) Everything works when it’s not an emergency. The test of your ideas: Does it work when it is an emergency? Chait: No; I’ve always been taken by that comment because what it’s saying is that our ideas are just a theological commitment. More of an aspiration and not something that you can actually trust to work in the real world. But nonetheless, that we should be guided by them for theological reasons and not for practical ones. Frum: One of the legacies of that Obama experience was—so the Obama stimulus was about $800 billion, if I remember correctly. About half of it in the form of immediate cash relief and about half of it in the form of spending, which was a big number at the time. In the Democratic world, that experience was remembered as: Obama didn’t do enough . And so Biden, who was confronting not a deflationary crisis the way Obama was, but an inflationary crisis, he spent much more and ran even bigger deficits—well, maybe they weren’t bigger deficits to the economy, because the government’s revenue hadn’t collapsed as much. But he ran very big deficits. And of course, this time the voices of conventional wisdom were correct; that Biden was spending too much, and he had overlearned the Obama experience that Obama had handled successfully and Biden handled less successfully. Chait: Obama understood that he needed to stimulate the economy more. I mean, as soon as he got the stimulus, he tried to get more stimulus. He got every dollar he could get out of Congress. You could make an argument that he could have gotten more if he tried different methods, but he was trying to get—he understood, first of all, the recession was deeper than they grasped at the time they passed the stimulus. So they calculated the size of the hole, and they figured out, Okay, so how close to filling up the hole can we get? And then it turns out the hole was even deeper than they thought. So then, they immediately were trying to get more money, and they did get more money. They got more tax credits; they pulled out more stimulus here and there. But they did not get enough stimulus, and the recovery was too slow. And that was the main lesson, that they needed to not repeat that mistake. But the problem is they just erred in the opposite direction under Biden. Frum: So the left theory of the Obama presidency is: Obama didn’t do enough, and therefore the working class got mad, and they voted for Trump, and it’s Obama’s fault. Chait: I mean, you can explain Trump’s victory through normal political arguments. You don’t need to summon this crisis of capitalism that produced Trump. It’s hard to win a third consecutive term for any party. Hillary Clinton was a less talented politician than Obama. She was challenged from the left by Bernie Sanders, and her response to that challenge was for herself to move leftward still. So the candidate who ran in 2016 under difficult conditions for any candidate was not running as Obama’s third term. But she was running significantly to the left of Obama’s third term with less political skills. Obama left office with a 60 percent approval rating. Obama, had he been able to run for president for a third time, would’ve wiped the floor with Donald Trump. There’s just no reason to believe that Donald Trump was a repudiation of Obama, who was and is very popular, and far more popular than Trump. Frum: I have a really brain-dead theory of what happened that ignores all the personalities and so on. Which: This is my theory of how Obama led to Trump. The economy returns to precrisis levels of output and employment in 2014. Pre the crisis of 2007, ’08. So we’re back at 2014 to where we were in 2007, although the growth trajectory is lower. At that point, respectable opinion says: Right; Obama’s been running these big deficits. This could lead to inflation if unchecked. Now is the time for the Federal Reserve to tighten interest rates. And that was not a crazy decision. That’s a very conventional, normal decision. The crisis is over. I mean, we’re back to where we were. Tighten now. And it turns out the economy was still, in 2014, not healthy yet. And when you tightened in 2014, instead of saying, Okay, the growth continues, as it did when you tightened in the middle ’80s, instead what happened is: The employment growth slows. And so you have very not-recessionary conditions in 2015, 2016, but disappointing conditions. People do not feel continuing improvement, and they weren’t just grateful to be pulled from the sea to the shore. They wanted to resume the normal, you know, trajectory from the shore. And that didn’t happen. And so the incumbent party lost, and then the Federal Reserve recognized its mistake, loosened in 2016, and the economy accelerated in 2017, 2018, 2019. We had three good years before the COVID pandemic. Chait: Right. They thought we were at capacity. There was a debate about: Are we at capacity? Are we about to hit the point of accelerating inflation in 2014? And we weren’t, and we found that out in Trump’s first term that there was actually plenty of slack left in the labor market, plenty of room to grow. You’re right. That was an important moment. And that could well have made the difference, because the 2016 election was so close. Just a little bit more growth in those last two [years] could have made the difference. A lot of things could have made the difference. But I would just point out in the overall macro-situation, Obama was popular. Obama’s popularity was not the problem. I mean, if he was even more popular, it would’ve helped more, but he was overall popular. Frum: Now in 2026, we have this attack on Obama from the left. He’s now become quite a demon figure. And explain to me—what is the left case in 2026 against Obama? Why is Obama now bad? Chait: Well, the main thing that they will say that Obama did badly was bailing out the banks in 2008. Obama’s 2008 bank bailout— Frum: 2009. 2009. Chait: No, no, no; 2008. Now, of course, the bank bailout did occur in 2008. Frum: Yeah. Chait: But Obama did not become president ’til 2009. But when I point this out, people will never believe me. I’ve been pointing this out for 15 years, and no one will believe me. So I think I just have to accept that I’m wrong, and that Barack Obama actually was president in 2008, and he’s therefore responsible for the bank bailout that occurred in 2008. Frum: I think the bank bailout was good. And whoever was president in 2008—which turns out to be maybe a more difficult question than … I’m sorry to have interrupted you, because I thought it was an easy question. But as you say—as with the question, Who was president in 2020?— it turns out to be quite hard. Chait: Yes. ( Chuckles .) Frum: So leaving aside the mysterious question of who was president in 2008, why is it, if you’re the left and you love [President] Franklin Delano Roosevelt, who saved the banks, why do you hate whoever was president in 2008, who saved the banks? Chait: Yeah. I’ve brought up this point many times. It’s very hard for me. I want to faithfully reproduce their criticisms; I don’t want to just be battling straw men. But it’s very hard for me on this point, because I feel like so little sense can be drawn from the criticisms they make. Like I said, the No. 1 point they make is the bank bailout. That’s by far the most common critique they make of Obama. The second most common they make is failing to jail anyone for the crimes of the financial crisis. What actually happened was, [the Obama administration] looked at it and said: Well, they didn’t commit any crimes. The problem is all this stuff was legal, so we need to change the laws. And so they passed the Dodd-Frank financial reforms, which were the strongest regulations of Wall Street since the 1930s. At the time, those reforms were celebrated by progressives. If you ask any of the progressive experts in financial regulation, they will say that’s a very powerful law; a set of reforms that were formative. It looked at all the problems of the financial crisis, really regulated all of them. It also created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. But [critics] blame Obama for not imprisoning anyone for activity that was only subsequently made illegal. So again, I’m sort of attacking arguments that sound like straw men, but these really are the most common attacks made on Obama. Frum: Go, take a step beyond the attacks. Because often when people say things, they are applying imperfect words to deep feelings. Okay, so maybe they don’t have good rationalizations, but where does it come from? What is the mentality that says, I revere Franklin Delano Roosevelt, but I hate Barack Obama ? Where does that mood come from? Where does, where does Bernie Sanders-ism, what is the emotional need that it meets? Chait: I think there was significant difference between Obama and the organized progressive movement. Do you remember when Obama’s spokesman derided the professional left? That was a somewhat notorious comment, but it really did capture a hostile relationship between the organized progressive movement and the Obama administration. And he thought that these organized progressive lobbies were unrealistic, didn’t have good ideas, and he had better ideas for messaging and for policy strategy. So they were always on the outs with him, and they resented that. Biden, by contrast, was so deeply enmeshed with the progressive movement—the “professional left,” as they were called under the Obama era—that it was almost impossible to draw any distance between them at all. Biden did whatever they wanted. And so even though Biden had dramatically less legislative success, the progressive movement really celebrated Biden’s administration all the way ’til the end, when they decided that now Gaza was the only thing that mattered, and Gaza was the reason that he was a failure. But really, up until that moment they were celebrating Biden as the heir to Roosevelt. Biden as the progressive hero, and Obama as the sad, weak appendage to the Reagan era. Frum: Is there something going on, too, that if you’re on the real left that you regard Trump as not the worst possible outcome? Because if you’re on the real left, Trump is obviously—it isn’t that they like him, but they know the working class, they will sooner or later see through the folly of Trump. Just as Hitler led to the triumph of communism in Germany, so—not to compare Trump to Hitler—but this is the thinking. The far right gets its turn; then we get our turn. We just need to exclude the middle, and then we win. Chait: This was also the thinking of the communist left in Weimar Germany, right? They saw Hitler’s constituency as their own constituency. They really thought that there was this fluidity between the far left and the far right. I don’t think that was correct at all. Frum: But at the intellectual level, there’s something to that. I mean, we all know people, and we could name them if we wanted to, who do seem to move very easily between far left and far right. And these are people who are very well educated, who care a lot about politics, care a lot about ideas. You’ll hear them say: I’m a progressive, but I feel at home when I talk to these ultra-MAGA people. We both hate bankers, we both hate Ukraine, we both hate Israel. We have so much in common. And they think, and that must apply at the voting level, where people vote for reasons that are less ideological. Chait: That’s right. It’s the same error. And that’s why in some level, you’re right that Trump’s election filled them with hope. That they really saw this proletarian uprising that they’ve been longing for but were dejected that was not happening, finally glimmers of it happening. Because you could see elements of Trump’s populist rhetoric as reflecting their own. So I think you’re spot on on that observation. Frum: So how much of your life do you spend defending the Obama legacy to people who want to detract it, from the left? Jonathan Chait: Too much. Too much. I’m planning to write something maybe early next year. I’ve gotta just put it all in one place. But It’s gotten to the point where I have this alternate history that only I and a handful of deranged lunatics are aware of. And we’re living in an alternate universe in which everyone else has settled on a completely different interpretation of what happened during those years. So I’ve gotta just put it all in one place, I think. Frum: Well, let me ask you about your native Michigan now, because these issues are being played out in real time. They’re both— Frum: And is there an incumbent senator in Michigan? Chait: No. Gary Peters is the incumbent Democrat who’s retiring, so there’s an open seat. Frum: How competitive a state is Michigan? Chait: It’s a slightly blue state, although Trump won it in 2024 and in 2016. So it’s very close at the presidential level. Democrats have usually won the Senate races and have usually won the gubernatorial races most of the time, but Donald Trump did win it a couple times. Frum: So now there’s an open Democratic nomination. There is a Republican candidate who’s competed before, who’s a strong candidate, who’s not a loony at all. Chait: Right. Frum: And the Democrats will soon vote to choose one of two candidates. So tell us about the two Democratic choices. Chait: There’s Haley Stevens, who’s a kind of center-left traditional Democrat. She’s just an amalgamation of the traditional center-left Democratic Party in the state of Michigan. Abdul El-Sayed is very left wing for the Democratic Party. He would be the most left-wing Democrat in the Senate, I think even to the left of Bernie Sanders. He would be as far left maybe as people like [U.S. Representatives] Ilhan Omar, Rashida Tlaib. He’s just across-the-board left on every issue, and has really emphasized opposition to Israel as a campaign theme. Frum: And he seems to be a less psychologically troubled person than Graham Platner. And although this is maybe invidious to say, probably more intelligent than Graham Platner. But I feel like recently, it’s like a gambler who’s on a winning streak and is just overplaying his hands. I’ll give you an example. Gretchen Whitmer endorsed Haley Stevens over the weekend. And he said this, and a lot of other leftists have said this, that he will become their standard-bearer. Bernie Sanders is getting old now. And if [El-Sayed] can win, he will prove something that they’ve never been able to demonstrate before—that a left-wing candidate can win in a purple state. Frum: One of the things that matters outside Michigan is the left has probably given away the Maine Senate seat. Vance and his program of Orbánism in the English language. Chait: Right. This is going to become the main proof point that’s being used in this interfactional war within the Democratic Party. Vance” ticket in 2028, at least we can have a consensus about the danger of the Jews. That would be— Chait: ( Laughs .) That’s right. Frum: America could be united. Vance means for the future of American democracy. Chait: Absolutely. Look, it’s, it’s an old problem, right? Frum: Where is Obama in all of this? It’s his legacy that is under attack. Both institutionally, but also quite personally. Will he stand up for himself in an argument?
